translations.text: The evangelist Luke wrote in Christ's book about the birth of John the Baptist, saying: "There was a devout servant of God named Zacharias, and his wife was called Elizabeth.
They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in his commandments and ordinances. They had no child together," and so on.
"All his clothing was woven from camel's hair, and his food was harsh. He drank no wine, and no mixed or brewed drink. He lived on fruit and wild honey and other poor foods."
"In the fifteenth year of the reign of the emperor Tiberius, the word of God came to John in the desert;
and he went out to where the people lived, and preached to the Jewish people a baptism for the forgiveness of sins, as it is written in the prophecy of Isaiah."
He proclaimed Christ's baptism as coming to all the faithful, in which there is forgiveness of sins through the Holy Spirit.
At God's direction John also baptized those of the Jewish people who came to him. But his baptism brought no forgiveness of any sin, because he was God's herald and not God.
He proclaimed the Saviour's coming to people with words, and his holy baptism with his own baptism, in which he baptized the sinless Son of God, who needed no forgiveness of any sin.
Rightly does God's Church honour this day, the feast of the birth of the great Baptist, because of the many wonders that took place at his birth.
God's archangel Gabriel announced to his father Zechariah his birth, and his high dignity, and his glorious way of life.
The child in his mother's womb recognized the voice of Mary, the Mother of God; and while still enclosed in the womb, with prophetic rejoicing, he signified the saving coming of our Redeemer.
By his birth he took away his mother's barrenness, and his name set free his father's tongue, which had been struck dumb because of his own unbelief.
The holy Church celebrates the birthdays of three people: the Saviour, who is God and man; John, his herald; and the blessed Mary, his mother.
In the case of other chosen people, who reached God's kingdom through martyrdom or through other holy merits, their last day,
which, once all their hardships were over, brought them forth victorious into eternal life, is the day we honour as their birthday.
and the day on which they were born into this present life we let pass unregarded, because they came here to hardships, and temptations, and various dangers.
God's servants remember the day that sent the saints, once their victory was won, away from all afflictions into eternal joy. That day is their true birth:
not tearful like the first one, but joyful, into eternal life. But we must honour Christ's birthday with great devotion, for through it our redemption came.
John is the end of the old law and the beginning of the new, just as the Saviour said of him,
"The old law and the prophets lasted until John's coming." After that, the preaching of the gospel began.
Now, because of his great holiness, his birth is honoured, just as the archangel promised his father with these words: "Many will rejoice at his birth."

Mary, the Mother of God, is like no one else, because she is both virgin and mother, and she gave birth to the one who created her and all creatures. So she is fully worthy to have her birth celebrated with honour.

The kinsfolk gave the child the name Zechariah, but the mother opposed them with words, and the mute father with writing; because the angel who had announced his coming had appointed for him, by God's command, the name John.
The dumb father could not tell his wife what name the angel had given the child, but the name became known to her through the revelation of God's Spirit.
Zacharias means 'Mindful of God,' and John means 'God's grace,' because he preached God's grace to people, and preached the coming of Christ, who guides the whole world with his grace.
He was sent ahead of the Lord, as the morning star goes ahead of the sun, as a herald goes ahead of a judge, as the Old Testament goes ahead of the New;
because the old law was like a shadow, and the New Testament is truth through the grace of the Saviour.
Christ and John were children of one year. On this day the barren mother gave birth to the great prophet John, who is praised with these words from Christ's mouth:
"Among the children of women no greater man has arisen than John the Baptist."

On Midwinter's Mass-day (Christmas Day) the holy maiden Mary gave birth to the Heavenly Prince. He is not counted among the children of women, because he is God's Son in the Godhead, and the Child of God and of a maiden through his humanity.
John fled the company of people in his youth, and in the wilderness he avoided sins by a strict way of life.
The Saviour remained among sinners, unstained by any sin. At that time the herald turned a great multitude of the people of Israel to their Creator by his preaching.
Daily the Lord turns countless souls from all nations to his faith, through the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit.
The holy gospel says of the Baptist that he went before the Saviour in the spirit and power of the prophet Elijah;
because he was his forerunner at the first coming, just as Elijah will be at the second, against Antichrist.
It is not without meaning that the herald's birth took place at the time when the earthly day is growing shorter, while at the time of the Lord's birth it is growing longer.
John himself revealed this meaning with these words: "It is fitting for Christ that he should increase, and for me that I should decrease."
John became known to people sooner than Christ did, through his glorious way of life, because Christ did not show his divine power until he had been thirty years in his human life.
At that time the people thought that he was a prophet, and that John was the Christ.
Then Christ revealed himself through great signs, and his fame grew throughout the whole world that he was true God, he who had earlier been thought a prophet.
John, truly, was decreasing in his fame, because he became known as a prophet and as the herald of the Heavenly Prince, he who a little earlier had been reckoned the Christ by uncertain supposition.
This decrease is signified by the shortening day at the time of his birth, and the lengthening day at the Saviour's birth signifies Christ's increasing power in his humanity.

Many prophets proclaimed in their prophecy that the Lord was to come, some from far off and some from near at hand. But John proclaimed his coming with words and also pointed him out with his finger, saying:
"Look now! Here goes the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world." Christ is called by many names.
He is called Wisdom, because the Father made all creatures through him. He is called Word, because a word is the manifestation of wisdom.
The evangelist John began his gospel account with the Word, saying, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
He is called the Lamb because of the innocence of the lamb's nature; and he, though guiltless, was offered in the manner of a lamb as a living sacrifice to his Father, for our redemption.
He is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, because through his divine strength he overcame the great devil by the victory of his passion.
The holy Baptist, of whom we are speaking, established a strict way of life, both in clothing and in food, as we told a little earlier;
because the ruling Saviour spoke thus about him: "From the days of John the kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it."

Every wise person knows that the old law was easier than Christ's ordinance is, because under it there was no great abstinence, nor the spiritual ways of life which Christ and his apostles later established.
The decree that a king issues through his ealdormen or reeves is one thing; his own proclamation made in his presence is another.
In this passage the kingdom of God means the holy Church, that is, all Christian people, who must earn the heavenly kingdom by force and with a determined mind.
How can it be without force and violence that anyone, through God's grace, subdues lustful nature with chastity?
Or who calms the anger of his mind with patience without hardship? Or who turns away pride with true humility?
Or who overcomes drunkenness with sobriety, or greed with generosity, without struggle?
But whoever, through God's help, changes his habits in this way with steadfastness is then made into another man;
…he is another through goodness, and the same through substance, and he then seizes the heavenly kingdom by force.
There are two kinds of abstinence: one bodily, the other spiritual.
The first is that each person should govern himself with moderation in food and drink, and manfully deny himself excessive eating.
Another kind of abstinence is more precious and more exalted, though the other is good: to govern the stirrings of one's mind with constant moderation, and to fight daily against vices,
The second is that he should chasten himself with the strictness of spiritual discipline, so that he subdues the fierce beasts of the eight chief sins as if with iron bits.
This abstinence is precious, and a glorious suffering in God's sight: to restrain evil thoughts and evil desires with one's own royal sceptre,
and to keep oneself from harmful speech and dangerous deeds, just as from deadly foods.
Whoever diligently practises these things will without doubt seize the promised kingdom with God and all his saints.
It is a great act of force that human beings, by humble merits, should gain the heavenly joy that the heavenly angels lost through pride.
We wish to speak further about the holy man John, to his honour and for our improvement.
The prophet Isaiah wrote of him that he is "the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of God, make his paths straight.
Every valley shall be filled, and every hill shall be brought low, and all crooked places shall be made straight, and rough places made smooth."
The prophet called him a voice because he went before Christ, who is called the Word: not a word such as people speak, but he is the Wisdom of the Father, and a word is the revealing of wisdom.

That Word is Almighty God, the Son with his Father. In every word a voice is heard before the word is fully spoken. Just as the voice goes before the word, so John went before the Saviour in the world;
because God the Father sent him before the face of his Son, so that he should prepare and make ready his way. So John called out these same words to people:
"Prepare God's way." The herald who preaches right faith and good works prepares the way for God to come into the hearts of those who listen.
God's way is prepared in people's hearts when they humbly hear the words of the Truth and are ready to keep the commandments of Life. Of this the Saviour said:
"He who loves me keeps my commandment, and my Father loves him, and we two will come to him and dwell with him."
His paths are made straight when, through good preaching, pure thoughts spring up in the minds of those who listen.
Valleys stand for the humble, and hills for the proud. At the Lord's coming the valleys were filled and the hills brought low, just as he himself said:
"Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted."

Just as water runs down from the hill and settles in the valley, so the Holy Spirit flees from the hearts of the proud and makes his dwelling in the humble, as the prophet said: "On whom does the Spirit of God rest but on the humble?"
The crooked places are made straight when the hearts of perverse people, which have been bent aside by the hooks of unrighteousness, are made level again by the measuring-rod of true righteousness.
Rough places are turned into smooth ways when angry and harsh minds turn to gentleness through receiving the heavenly grace.
It would take too long for us to relate, and for you to hear, all the depths of the great Baptist's preaching:

how with severe rebuke and stern warning he turned the hard-hearted Jewish people toward the way of life, and after his martyrdom announced Christ's coming to the inhabitants of hell, just as in his lifetime he had boldly proclaimed to mankind, with a loud voice, its own redemption.
Let us now pray to the ruling Savior that, through the intercession of his great Forerunner and Baptist,
he may have mercy on us in this present life and lead us to the eternal life. To him be glory and praise, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
